questions.q: What does running `git add` on a previously conflicted file tell Git?
options: To delete the file entirely
To undo the merge completely
Nothing — add has no special meaning during a conflict
That this file's conflict is now resolved and ready to be included in the merge commit
questions.explain: Staging a conflicted file after editing it is exactly how you tell Git the conflict in that file has been resolved.

questions.q: What is a "commit" in version control terms?
options: A saved, timestamped, attributed snapshot of the project at a point in time
A synonym for deleting a file
A password required to open the repository
A type of merge conflict
questions.explain: A commit is the core unit of history in a VCS — a recorded snapshot you can always return to.

questions.q: Why do commits replayed by `git rebase` get new commit hashes, even when the code changes are identical?
options: Because rebase deletes the original commits and writes brand-new commits with a different base, which changes the hash
Git randomly reassigns hashes for no reason
Rebase doesn't actually change hashes — this is a myth
Hashes only change if you add the --force flag
questions.explain: A commit's hash is derived partly from its parent commit, so replaying it onto a different base necessarily produces a new commit with a new hash.

questions.q: What are the three states a tracked file moves through in Git?
options: Draft, Review, Published
Local, Remote, Archived
Working directory, staging area, repository
Open, Staged, Closed
questions.explain: A file is edited in the working directory, marked with git add into the staging area, then permanently recorded via git commit into the repository.

questions.q: What does GitHub add on top of plain Git?
options: GitHub replaces Git entirely with a different system
Nothing — GitHub and Git are the exact same product
Hosting for Git repositories, plus collaboration tools like pull requests, code review, issues, and project boards
GitHub is only a text editor for writing code
questions.explain: Git is the version control system itself; GitHub hosts repositories and adds a collaboration layer on top.

questions.q: What is a GitHub Issue typically used for, as distinct from a pull request?
options: Tracking a bug report, feature request, task, or question — the work before a specific code change exists, unlike a PR which proposes an actual change
Issues and pull requests are exactly the same thing
Issues are only for reporting problems with GitHub itself, not a project's own code
Issues automatically write the code needed to fix them
questions.explain: Issues are GitHub's lightweight tracker for work items; a pull request is the specific code change that (often) resolves one.

questions.q: What is a pull request, fundamentally?
options: A GitHub feature: a request to merge one branch into another that opens a space for discussion, checks, and review before the merge happens
A Git command that merges branches automatically with no review
A way to permanently delete a branch
A built-in part of Git itself, required before any merge
questions.explain: Pull requests are a GitHub (not Git) concept — git merge doesn't require one; PRs add a review checkpoint on top of Git.

questions.q: What does `git push -u origin main` set up that a plain `git push` doesn't, the first time you push a new branch?
options: It deletes the local branch after pushing
It links the local branch to that remote branch (the "upstream"), so future git push/pull calls know where to go without repeating the remote and branch name
It makes the branch private
It force-overwrites the remote's history
questions.explain: The --set-upstream flag records the tracking relationship, simplifying every push and pull afterward.

questions.q: Why do you need to add the original repository as an 'upstream' remote and periodically merge from it?
options: Because a fork doesn't automatically stay in sync with changes made to the original repository over time
Because GitHub deletes forks that aren't synced within a week
Because it's required before you can open any pull request
Because forks are read-only until synced
questions.explain: A fork is a snapshot at the time it was created; it won't pick up later changes to the original repo unless you explicitly fetch and merge from an upstream remote.

questions.q: How does trunk-based development keep merge conflicts manageable?
options: By disabling merge conflicts entirely in Git settings
By never allowing more than one developer to work at a time
By requiring every branch to be reviewed by five people
By keeping feature branches short-lived, so nobody is reconciling weeks of divergence
questions.explain: Because branches merge back within a day or two in trunk-based development, there's far less time for main and a branch to diverge.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is "blame" a somewhat misleading name for the command?
options: Because it only works on deleted files
Because it actually deletes the blamed commit
Because its real use is finding the fastest path to the reasoning behind a line, not assigning fault
Because it requires administrator access
questions.explain: The lesson frames git blame as a way to trace a line back to the commit message, PR, or ticket that explains why it's written that way — not a fault-finder.

questions.q: What is a GitHub Release, relative to a tag?
options: A completely unrelated feature with no connection to tags
A wrapper around a tag that adds release notes, source archives, and optional build artifacts
A replacement for tags that makes them obsolete
A tag that can only be created through the command line, never the web UI
questions.explain: A Release wraps an existing (or newly created) tag with documentation and downloadable assets, without changing what the tag itself points to.

questions.q: What does a pull request's Checks tab show?
options: The PR author's commit history on unrelated repositories
Only the PR's title and description
A list of every other open PR in the repository
A rolled-up view of every workflow run triggered by that PR's commits, in one place
questions.explain: The Checks tab aggregates every check that ran against a PR's commits, letting you inspect any individual commit's results.

questions.q: What is the one-word difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
options: There is no real difference — they're interchangeable terms
Delivery makes every passing change release-ready but a human still approves the release; Deployment ships it automatically with no approval step
Delivery only works with Python; Deployment only works with JavaScript
Deployment is slower than Delivery by design
questions.explain: The practical difference is the final manual approval step: Delivery stops just short of shipping, Deployment removes that click entirely.

questions.q: In `if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, what does this condition specifically require?
options: Any event at all, on any branch
The workflow must be manually triggered by a human
Only that a pull request exists, regardless of branch
The event must be a push (not a pull_request), AND the branch being pushed to must literally be main
questions.explain: Both conditions must be true: the triggering event is a push, and that push landed specifically on the main branch — which together describe a real merge to main.

questions.q: What are the three core pieces that make up a GitHub Actions workflow file?
options: header, body, footer
source, target, and destination
on (the trigger), jobs (units of work), and steps (ordered commands inside a job)
install, build, and ship
questions.explain: A workflow defines what event triggers it (on), one or more jobs that each run on their own fresh VM, and the ordered steps within each job.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should you show first when presenting your capstone in an interview or portfolio review?
options: A slide deck describing the project without showing the repository itself
The commit graph and branch history, proving a real feature branch was merged through a real pull request
An unrelated sample project instead of your own
The repository's README with no code or history shown
questions.explain: The lesson recommends starting with the commit graph and branch history because it visually proves the workflow is real, before discussing anything else.

questions.q: What must be true about the CI workflow's deploy job, according to the brief?
options: It must deploy before the tests even run
It should run on every single commit to every branch
It should never actually be configured, only described
It must be gated by github.event_name and github.ref so it only runs on a real merge to main
questions.explain: Consistent with Lesson 20, the deploy job must be conditioned to fire only on a real push/merge to main, not on every push or pull request.
